summary:
I've been building a Japanese-learning app for myself, mostly as an excuse to get serious about the language. The core is a grammar engine that treats sentences as data: a few dozen base words expand out into a couple hundred grammatical frames, which get combined into thousands of generated practice sentences, each checked for whether it's actually readable at the learner's current vocabulary.

Most of the interesting work has been finding bugs that don't look like bugs — tests that pass while checking nothing. One example: a "pick the right reply" drill deduplicated its multiple-choice options by an internal ID instead of the displayed text, so for a chunk of exchanges all four options ended up saying the same correct answer. Over 40% of those boards were literally impossible to get wrong, and every test stayed green because nothing about the code was malformed — it just wasn't testing the thing that mattered. I've started treating a passing test suite as a claim to verify, not a fact, especially anywhere a hand-written list is standing in for something that should be derived from the data.

Same theme on the audio side. I generate pronunciation clips for a few hundred vocabulary words through a local text-to-speech engine, and some Japanese homographs — a bare kana string can read as two different words — will silently synthesize the wrong one. I added a check that resynthesizes each clip's transcription and compares it back against the intended word before anything ships; it caught three mismatched clips out of around 340, all cases where the reading engine had guessed wrong on an isolated kana string that only reads correctly with its kanji attached.

The rest is fairly ordinary web app work — SQLite-backed multi-user state, spaced-repetition scheduling, a fair amount of frontend for drills and progress tracking — but the debugging has been the part worth remembering: almost every real defect here was a plausible-looking pass, not a crash.
